## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes two methods for estimating canopy cover (the
proportion of the sky obscured by vegetation when viewed from below):
the convex spherical densiometer and hemispherical (fisheye)
photography. Canopy cover is a key variable in stream habitat
assessments (SWAMP protocol), forest ecology, microclimate studies,
and solar radiation modeling. Separating this SOP from
[SOP-F304](SOP-F304-stream-physical-habitat.qmd) allows the methods
to be applied in any habitat, not just stream reaches [@jennings1999;
@lemmon1956].


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Measurement of overhead canopy cover in forests,
  riparian corridors, oak woodlands, restoration sites, and any
  habitat where tree or tall shrub canopy is present; includes both
  the spherical densiometer method and hemispherical photography
- **Does not apply to:** Canopy closure measured by line-intercept or
  vertical projection methods (see
  [SOP-F603](SOP-F603-vegetation-transect-surveys.qmd)); leaf area
  index (see [SOP-F605](SOP-F605-leaf-area-index.qmd)); remote sensing
  canopy cover from aerial or satellite imagery
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites with tree or tall shrub cover


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Specify method and number of measurement points         |
| Trained Personnel | Perform measurements per this SOP                       |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent measurement        |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Looking upward while walking increases trip and fall
  risk. Stop walking before looking up.
- **Biological:** Ticks, poison oak, and snakes in forested and
  riparian habitats.
- **Environmental:** Bright sunlight reflecting off the densiometer
  can cause glare. Wear sunglasses when not actively reading the
  instrument.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Long pants
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
- [ ] Tick repellent (riparian and woodland sites)

### Emergency Procedures

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd).


## 5. Equipment and Materials

### Method A: Spherical Densiometer

| Item                                  | Notes                                    |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Convex spherical densiometer (Forestry Suppliers Model A or equivalent) | Concave models also exist; specify which model is used |
| Bubble level (built into the densiometer) | Essential for consistent readings    |
| Field notebook or data sheet          | For recording dot counts                 |
| Compass                               | For orienting the four cardinal readings |

### Method B: Hemispherical Photography

| Item                                  | Notes                                    |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Camera with fisheye lens              | Full-frame fisheye (180 degrees circular) preferred; or smartphone with clip-on fisheye lens |
| Self-leveling tripod or monopod       | Camera must be level and facing directly upward |
| Bubble level (hot-shoe mounted or tripod-integrated) | For leveling the camera |
| Gray card or exposure reference       | For consistent exposure settings         |
| Laptop with canopy analysis software  | Gap Light Analyzer (GLA), hemIMAGE, or ImageJ with the Hemispherical plugin |
| GPS unit                              | Per [SOP-F006](SOP-F006-gps-site-navigation.qmd) |


## 6. Procedure

### 6.1 Measurement Point Selection

Canopy cover measurements are typically taken at systematic intervals
along a transect or at the center and edges of fixed-area plots.

- **Stream habitat surveys (SWAMP):** Measure at 11 equally spaced
  points along each cross-section transect (left bank, center, right
  bank at each of the main transect positions). See
  [SOP-F304](SOP-F304-stream-physical-habitat.qmd).
- **Forest inventory plots:** Measure at the plot center and at 4
  points on the plot boundary (N, E, S, W).
- **Transect-based surveys:** Measure at regular intervals (e.g.,
  every 10 m or 25 m along a 50 m transect).

Record the GPS coordinates of each measurement point or its position
along the transect.

### 6.2 Method A: Convex Spherical Densiometer

The densiometer has a convex mirror with an etched grid. The observer
counts the number of grid intersections that are open to the sky
(not obstructed by vegetation) in each of four cardinal directions
[@lemmon1956; @strickler1959].

1. Hold the densiometer at elbow height (approximately 30--40 cm in
   front of your body), level it using the bubble level.
2. Position your head so that its reflection is just outside the grid
   area. This ensures a consistent viewing angle.
3. Face **north**. Imagine the grid divided into 24 squares (4 rows x
   6 columns). At each of the 24 grid intersections, determine whether
   the sky or vegetation is reflected. Count the number of open (sky)
   intersections. Record this count.
4. Rotate 90 degrees and face **east**. Repeat the count.
5. Repeat for **south** and **west**.
6. Calculate canopy cover:

$$
\text{Canopy openness (\%)} = \frac{\text{sum of 4 counts}}{96} \times 100
$$

$$
\text{Canopy cover (\%)} = 100 - \text{canopy openness (\%)}
$$

where 96 is the total number of possible open points across 4
directions (24 per direction x 4 directions).

::: {.callout-important}
The convex densiometer systematically overestimates canopy openness
compared to hemispherical photography because of the wide-angle optics
and the observer's head position [@cook1995]. Report the method used
alongside all canopy cover values, and do not mix methods within a
dataset.
:::

### 6.3 Method B: Hemispherical Photography

Hemispherical photographs capture a 180-degree view of the canopy and
are analyzed digitally to classify sky vs. canopy pixels [@frazer2001].

**In the field:**

1. Mount the camera on the tripod at breast height (1.37 m) or at a
   height specified by the project protocol.
2. Level the camera using the bubble level. The lens must point directly
   upward (zenith).
3. Orient the top of the camera toward magnetic north. Record the
   declination if relevant.
4. Set the camera to manual exposure. Bracket the exposure (take 3
   photos: one at the metered exposure, one stop under, one stop
   over) to ensure at least one well-exposed image.
5. Shoot in overcast or uniformly cloudy conditions whenever possible.
   Direct sunlight produces bright spots that confound automatic
   thresholding.
6. Include a gray card in one reference photo per site for exposure
   calibration.
7. Record the photo number, GPS coordinates, date, time, and sky
   conditions in the field notebook.

**In the lab:**

1. Import images into canopy analysis software (Gap Light Analyzer,
   hemIMAGE, or ImageJ with the Hemispherical plugin).
2. Register the image (set lens projection, define the circular
   boundary, orient to north).
3. Apply a binary threshold to classify each pixel as sky (white) or
   canopy (black). Adjust the threshold manually if automated
   thresholding produces obvious errors.
4. The software calculates canopy openness, canopy cover, leaf area
   index (effective), and gap fraction by zenith angle.
5. Export results as a `.csv` file. Save to the project repository
   under `data/canopy/`.

### 6.4 Reporting

Report canopy cover values with the following metadata:

- Method (densiometer or hemispherical photography)
- Instrument model (densiometer type; camera and lens model)
- Measurement height above ground
- Date, time, and sky conditions
- Software and thresholding method (for photography)
- Number of measurement points and their spatial arrangement


## 7. Quality Control

- **Densiometer:** Have two observers independently read the same point.
  Readings should agree within 5 percentage points. If they disagree
  by more than 10 points, re-read together to identify the source of
  discrepancy.
- **Hemispherical photography:** Process the same image twice using
  different threshold values (+/- 10 units). If the resulting canopy
  cover differs by more than 5 percentage points, the image may be
  poorly exposed; re-shoot if possible.
- At a subset of sites, measure canopy cover with both methods and
  report the comparison. This allows future users to relate datasets
  collected with different methods.
- Record the observer's name with every densiometer measurement;
  observer bias is the largest error source.

## 10. Training Record

Before measuring canopy cover independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Demonstrate correct densiometer technique (leveling, head position,
   cardinal-direction counts) with results within 5 percentage points
   of the trainer's reading on at least 5 test points
3. If using hemispherical photography, demonstrate camera setup,
   exposure bracketing, and image analysis in the lab
4. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
